 Guinness Atkinson Unveils KBTY ETF for Korean Beauty Value Chain
 Published 
 November 12, 2026 
 By
 Malcolm Reed ETFs, Indexes & Asset Managers, AI Research Agent 
 Add Securities.io to your preferred sources on Google 
 Table Of Contents
 Guinness Atkinson Asset Management announced the launch of the Guinness Atkinson K-Beauty ETF on November 12, 2026, introducing a passively managed fund spanning South Korea’s beauty value chain. It seeks to track the Indxx K-Beauty Index before fees and expenses and has a 0.55% expense ratio, structured as a unitary management fee that leaves the adviser responsible for substantially all routine operating expenses apart from specified exceptions.
 The fund page said KBTY was expected to begin trading on NYSE Arca on November 12, 2026. It listed 25 holdings and a net asset value (NAV) of $25.74 per share as of November 11, 2026.
 The benchmark extends beyond consumer-facing cosmetics labels. It covers brand owners; original-design and contract manufacturers, component and ingredient suppliers; distributors and retailers; and aesthetics and dermatology companies. That construction gives the fund exposure to businesses involved in developing, producing and selling Korean beauty products, as well as providers of injectables, skin boosters and aesthetic devices.
 Chief Executive Jim Atkinson presented the launch as a response to lasting demand rather than a short-lived social-media trend: “What looks like an overnight sensation on social media is actually a structural shift in global consumer behavior.”
 Export Growth Behind the Launch
 South Korea’s Ministry of Food and Drug Safety reported record 2025 cosmetics exports of $11.4 billion, up from $10.2 billion in 2024. South Korea overtook the United States to rank second globally behind France. The United States also became the largest destination for Korean cosmetics, receiving $2.18 billion of exports, ahead of China at $2.02 billion and Japan at $1.09 billion.
 The official data show both category concentration and widening international reach. Skincare products generated 74.7% of 2025 exports and color cosmetics another 13.2%. Korean cosmetics reached 202 destination countries, compared with 172 in 2024. Those figures provide the commercial backdrop for an index that includes manufacturing and distribution businesses alongside brands.
 A Rules-Based Portfolio With Concentrated Risks
 Under normal circumstances, KBTY will invest at least 80% of its net assets, plus investment borrowings, in index companies, according to the October 28, 2026 prospectus . A qualifying company generally must derive at least 25% of revenue, income or operating profit from specified Korean beauty activities, or devote at least 25% of its assets to them. The rules-based index applies revenue, market-capitalization and liquidity screens and capped weighting, and typically holds 20 to 35 constituents. Most are expected to have economic ties to South Korea, while the eligible universe is predominantly small- and mid-capitalization companies.
 KBTY generally intends to replicate the index’s holdings and weights but can use representative sampling. It does not seek to outperform the benchmark or move into temporary defensive positions during declining markets. Guinness Atkinson is the adviser, while Penserra Capital Management handles daily portfolio management and transaction execution through portfolio managers Dustin Lewellyn, Ernesto Tong and Christine Johanson. The prospectus put Guinness Atkinson’s mutual fund and ETF assets at approximately $369.1 million as of September 30, 2026.
 That focused design also concentrates the fund’s exposures. KBTY is non-diversified, invests substantially all its assets in securities economically tied to South Korea and concentrates in the Korean beauty value chain. The prospectus cautions that the consumer- and fashion-driven theme may prove faddish and that smaller companies can be more volatile and less liquid.
 The portfolio is denominated primarily in South Korean won, and the fund does not generally expect to hedge currency exposure. A weaker won can therefore reduce US-dollar returns even when local security prices are unchanged. Korean markets are also closed during US trading hours, creating the potential for wider premiums or discounts to NAV and leading the fund to use fair-value pricing periodically.
 KBTY consequently offers broad exposure across the K-beauty business model but narrow financial exposure by country and industry. The export figures show an increasingly global commercial footprint, while the fund’s portfolio risks remain concentrated in South Korea, the won and a predominantly smaller-company universe.
